overview: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple at Jamalapuram, in Yerrupalem Mandal of Khammam District, Telangana, is popularly known as 'Telangana Chinna Tirupati', 'Khammam Chinna Tirupati' or 'Telangana Tirupati', reflecting devotees' belief that the deity here is comparably powerful and auspicious to Lord Venkateswara at Tirumala. The presiding deity is a self-manifested (Swayambhu) form of Lord Vishnu, worshipped as 'Balaji' in stone (vigraha) form with consorts Sri Padmavathi and Sri Alamelu (Alivelu) Ammavaru. Recognised as a Swayam Vyakta kshetra (per the official Telangana Tourism portal), it is one of the older Vaishnavite shrines in Khammam district — believed to be over 800–850 years old per the main priest (Uppala Srinivasa Sarma) and 'over 1,000 years old' per tourism sources. It was visited by the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra on his way to Tiruvuru and renovated in the early 16th century by Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya en route to Kondapalli fort during his 'Jaitra Yatra'. A statue of Sri Krishnadevaraya stands near the Pongali Mandapam (installed c. 2010 to mark the 500th anniversary of his coronation). The temple draws large crowds, especially on Saturdays and during Brahmotsavam, Vaikunta Ekadasi and Dwadasi.
summary: Sri Venkateswara Swamy Temple at Jamalapuram (Yerrupalem Mandal, Khammam district, Telangana) is a Vaishnavite shrine to a Swayambhu Venkateswara ('Balaji') with consorts Padmavathi and Alamelu, popularly called 'Telangana Chinna Tirupati'. Believed to be 800–1,000+ years old (per the main priest and tourism sources), it was visited by the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra and renovated by Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya in the early 16th century. Two founding legends link it to sage Jabali's penance at Suchi Gutta (Soochi Giri) and to the devotee Uppala Yagnanarayana Sharma / his descendant Uppala Akku Bhatlu, after whom the deity is said to have self-manifested. The temple features a five-tier Gopuram, a Pedda Cheruvu tank, sub-shrines to Shiva, Ganesh, Ayyappa and Hanuman, and a statue of Sri Krishnadevaraya. It is recognised by the official Telangana Tourism portal as a Swayam Vyakta kshetra and is busiest on Saturdays and during Brahmotsavam and Vaikunta Ekadasi.

history.content: The temple is one of the older Vaishnavite shrines in Khammam district. Per the main priest Uppala Srinivasa Sarma (quoted in 2017 press reports), it is believed to be more than 800–850 years old; some tourism sources describe it as 'over 1,000 years old' — both estimates are widely repeated. The temple is said to have been visited by the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra on his way to Tiruvuru, and later renovated by the Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya, who offered prayers here en route to Kondapalli fort during his military campaign known as the 'Jaitra Yatra'. The temple is also described as having flourished as a gurukulam (seat of learning) under the sage Jabali. Around 2010, a statue of Sri Krishnadevaraya was installed near the Pongali Mandapam as part of celebrations marking the 500th anniversary of his coronation. Located in a pollution-free area surrounded by lush green hills and the Pedda Cheruvu (temple tank), the temple is recognised as a Swayam Vyakta kshetra on the official Telangana Tourism portal.

history.content: Two versions of the temple's founding legend are repeated across sources; both are presented as they could not be reconciled into a single canonical account from an official source. (1) Jabali Maharshi legend: the sage performed penance at a hillock here called Suchi Gutta (Soochi Giri), after which he was blessed with a vision of Lord Vishnu, who manifested as an icon at the spot. (2) Uppala Yagnanarayana Sharma / Akku Bhatlu legend: a devotee named Uppala Yagnanarayana Sharma paused here during a Kashi pilgrimage and settled; he felt a mysterious pull, and Lord Venkateswara came as a child to play with cattlemen every day. If anyone asked the child's name and place, he would answer 'your signature is my name, your location is my place'. Yagnanarayana Sharma eventually recognised the child and climbed to the top of the hill to worship him, where he discovered the Lord Venkateswara icon and inscriptions on the stone. A related version of the legend: his sixth descendant Uppala Akku Bhatlu — unable to climb the hill — prayed for guidance, and Lord Venkateswara instructed him to descend without looking back so the Lord could follow; Akku Bhatlu turned on hearing a loud sound, at which point the deity manifested (Swayambhu) at that spot.

Uppala Akku Bhatlu, a later descendant, was instructed by the Lord to descend the hill without looking back; on turning at a loud sound, the deity self-manifested (Swayambhu) at that spot.

sthala_puranam: Per temple lore (recorded only in tourism/blog sources), sage Jabali performed penance at the Suchi Gutta (Soochi Giri) hillock here and was blessed with a vision of Lord Vishnu, who manifested as a Swayambhu icon. An alternate legend holds that the devotee Uppala Yagnanarayana Sharma paused here during a Kashi pilgrimage, felt a mysterious pull, and settled; Lord Venkateswara came as a child to play with cattlemen every day, eventually revealing himself. A related version says his descendant Uppala Akku Bhatlu was instructed by Lord Venkateswara to descend the hill without looking back; on turning at a loud sound, the deity self-manifested (Swayambhu) at that spot. The temple is thus a Swayambhu / Swayam Vyakta kshetra, likened to Tirumala as 'Telangana Chinna Tirupati'.
religious_significance: Popularly known as 'Telangana Chinna Tirupati' / 'Khammam Chinna Tirupati', because devotees consider the deity comparably powerful and auspicious to Lord Venkateswara at Tirumala, and the temple shares the Swayambhu Venkateswara tradition. It is recognised as a Swayambhu / 'Swayam Vyakta' kshetra by the official Telangana Tourism portal. Some sources describe it as the most prominent Vaishnavite shrine in Khammam district (this superlative is asserted, not officially verified).
spiritual_significance: Devotees believe darshan and puja here lead to the fulfilment of wishes, akin to beliefs about the Tirumala Venkateswara temple. Saturdays are especially popular for worship (per the official Telangana Tourism portal). Passing through the temple's Vaikunta Dwaram on Vaikunta Ekadasi / Dwadasi is believed to grant spiritual passage to Vaikunta, Lord Vishnu's abode. The temple's serene, pollution-free, green-hilled setting is cited as conducive to peaceful meditation.

architecture: The temple features a five-tier Gopuram (entrance tower) with a Dhwaja Stambham (flag post) placed within it, and a Pongali Mandapam. The temple tank is known locally as Pedda Cheruvu. The complex follows South Indian temple architectural style and includes sub-shrines dedicated to Sri Padmavathi Ammavaru, Sri Alamelu (Alivelu / Alimelu Manga) Ammavaru, Lord Shiva (Sivalayam), Lord Ganesh, Lord Ayyappa, and Lord Hanuman / Anjaneya Swamy. A statue of Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya was installed near the Pongali Mandapam around 2010 as part of the 500th coronation anniversary celebrations. The temple is located amidst pleasant weather surrounded by lush green hills on the Telangana-AP border, which contributes to the calm atmosphere of the complex.

Per general Telugu temple convention, men typically wear dhoti or simple attire (often removing the shirt at the inner sanctum); women wear sarees or salwar suits. accommodation.availability: No temple-managed guest houses, cottages or choultries could be confirmed. The temple is in a rural village setting with limited on-site lodging. The official Telangana Tourism portal notes that a few hotels close to the temple offer limited cuisine during darshan timings, and recommends staying overnight in Khammam town (~75–86 km away) rather than at Jamalapuram, treating it as a day-trip pilgrimage.
accommodation.booking_process: No temple-run booking system confirmed; book private accommodation in Khammam town.

best_time_to_visit: Saturdays are especially popular (per Telangana Tourism). Brahmotsavam, Vaikunta Ekadasi/Dwadasi, and monthly Ekadasi days draw the heaviest crowds; weekends are busier than weekdays. For a quieter visit, choose weekday mornings. October to March is the most pleasant weather window for the surrounding green-hilled region.

It is said to have been visited by the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra and later renovated by the Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya, who prayed here en route to Kondapalli fort during his 'Jaitra Yatra'; a statue of him was installed near the Pongali Mandapam c. 2010 to mark the 500th anniversary of his coronation. travel_guide.en: Jamalapuram is in Yerrupalem Mandal, Khammam district, about 75 to 86 kilometres from Khammam town and roughly 52 to 56 kilometres from Vijayawada (the most geographically plausible distance — Yerrupalem is on the Telangana-AP border along NH65). faq.question: What are the temple's darshan timings?
faq.answer: Reported timings vary by source but generally fall within 5:00/6:00 AM–12:00/1:00 PM (morning) and 3:00/4:00 PM–7:30/9:00 PM (evening). The most authoritative single source (Trip.com) gives 6:00 AM–1:00 PM and 3:00 PM–7:30 PM with structured breaks. Confirm exact hours locally.

faq.question: Is there an entry fee?
faq.answer: General darshan is reported to be free of charge by an independent travel guide; this could not be cross-verified against an official source.

faq.question: Who is the presiding deity?
faq.answer: Lord Venkateswara (Balaji), a self-manifested (Swayambhu) form of Lord Vishnu in stone (vigraha) form, with consorts Sri Padmavathi Ammavaru and Sri Alamelu Ammavaru.

faq.question: Why is it called 'Telangana Chinna Tirupati'?
faq.answer: Because devotees consider the deity here comparably powerful and auspicious to Lord Venkateswara at Tirumala (Tirupati), and the temple shares the Swayambhu Venkateswara worship tradition. The temple is officially recognised as a Swayam Vyakta kshetra by the Telangana Tourism portal.

faq.question: How old is the temple?
faq.answer: Estimates vary: the main priest Uppala Srinivasa Sarma (cited in 2017) described it as more than 800–850 years old, while some tourism sources say 'over 1,000 years old'. The structure was significantly renovated in the early 16th century under Vijayanagara Emperor Sri Krishnadevaraya.

faq.question: How do I get to Jamalapuram?
faq.answer: By road via bus from Khammam (~75–86 km) or Vijayawada (~52–56 km, the most geographically plausible figure — Yerrupalem is on the Telangana-AP border along NH65). By rail to Errupalem (Yerrupalem) station (~6–7.5 km); the Krishna Express and Golconda Express pass through. By air via Gannavaram Airport, Vijayawada (~52–73 km). Hyderabad is ~260 km away.

faq.question: Is accommodation available at the temple?
faq.answer: No temple-managed guest house or choultry could be confirmed. The official tourism portal recommends staying overnight in Khammam town rather than at Jamalapuram, as on-site lodging is limited. Multiple visitor reviews note the area is 'not much developed' for food and stay.

faq.question: What are the major festivals?
faq.answer: Brahmotsavam (annual, ~9 days), Vaikunta Ekadasi / Dwadasi (Margashirsha, Nov–Dec, with passage through Vaikunta Dwaram), Sri Rama Navami, Maha Shivaratri, Sri Krishna Janmashtami, Navaratri / Durga Puja, and Akshaya Tritiya. Saturdays are the most popular weekly day for worship.

faq.question: Can non-Hindus or first-time visitors attend?
faq.answer: Yes; per an independent FAQ source the temple is open to all visitors and devotees irrespective of creed or caste (not confirmed by an official notice).

faq.question: Is there an official website or online seva booking?
faq.answer: No dedicated official temple website or online booking portal could be verified. Information is available via the official Telangana Tourism portal (tourism.telangana.gov.in) and the Khammam district government portal (khammam.telangana.gov.in/tourism/).

faq.question: What is the legend of Suchi Gutta and sage Jabali?
faq.answer: Per temple tradition, sage Jabali performed penance at the Suchi Gutta (Soochi Giri) hillock at the temple site and was blessed with a vision of Lord Vishnu, who manifested as an icon. The hillock is still associated with the temple and is visited by devotees as part of the pilgrimage.
